issues.legal_issue: Civil courts lack jurisdiction over a possession suit when deciding it requires determining who is the lawful ryot and that determination is exclusively assigned to a settlement authority whose decision is final.
material_facts: The respondents brought civil suits seeking possession and mesne profits from the appellants, who were in possession as sub-tenants.
After the estate vested in the State, deciding the suits required determining who was the lawful ryot of the land.
The governing law assigned that determination to the Settlement Officer and made the officer’s decision final and not open to challenge in court.
issues.conclusion: The civil courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the suits because determining the lawful ryot was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Settlement Officer. The appeals were allowed, and the order returning the plaints for presentation to the proper court was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 56(1) and (2) of the Madras Estates Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari Act, 1948, questions assigned to the Settlement Officer, including who is the lawful ryot, are for that officer to decide, and the finality of the officer’s decision ousts civil court jurisdiction over those questions. The Court applied Muddada Chayana v. Karnam Narayana and Oduru Chenchulakshamamma v. Duvvuru Reddy, which approved the view in Munuswami Naidu (dead) v. R. Venkata Reddy and rejected the earlier view in Cherukhuru Muthayya v. Gadde Gopalakrishnayya.

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A party brought a civil suit seeking possession of land from another party.
predicates.ryot_status_determination_required: Resolving the suit required determining who was the lawful ryot of the land.
predicates.settlement_authority_has_exclusive_final: The governing law assigned the ryot-status determination to a settlement authority and made its decision final and not challengeable in court.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks possession, requires a determination of lawful ryot status, and that determination is assigned exclusively and finally to a settlement authority, the civil court lacks jurisdiction.
